extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (Office personnel)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining novelty and nonobviousness under pre‑AIA and AIA versions of 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103, including when to apply KSR obviousness rationales, how to treat teaching away, joint research/common ownership exceptions, grace periods, and effective filing dates. Intended to help examiners determine applicable statutory provisions and to evaluate prior art and obviousness rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious‑to‑try rationale for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the prior art makes a finite number of identified, predictable solutions available and a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success in trying those options, the fact that an invention was 'obvious to try' may show the invention was obvious under § 103 (KSR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR: 'A person of ordinary skill has good reason to pursue the known options within his or her technical grasp. If this leads to the anticipated success, it is likely that product [was] not of innovation but of ordinary skill and common sense.' But the admonition that 'obvious to try' is not the standard has been directed at cases where (1) one would vary many parameters or try numerous possible choices with no indication which parameters are critical or which choices are likely to be successful, or (2) the prior art gives only general guidance about a promising field of experimentation and not specific direction as to how to achieve the claimed invention (see In re O'Farrell). Examiners should apply 'obvious to try' only where the situation meets KSR's predictable/finite/reasonable expectation of success criteria; avoid relying on it where the prior art suggests broad exploration or numerous blind trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion or motivation to combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: A suggestion or motivation to combine prior art references is an appropriate method for determining obviousness under § 103, but it is only one of multiple valid rationales consistent with Graham and KSR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR identified several exemplary rationales to support obviousness; see MPEP § 2141 and § 2143. Examiners may rely on an explicit suggestion/motivation in the prior art, on the predictable use of known elements according to their established functions, or other rationales laid out in case law, but must articulate the rationale for combining references when making a rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: References that teach away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference that 'teaches away' from the claimed invention is a significant factor in assessing obviousness; such teachings can weigh against a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'nature of the teaching is highly relevant and must be weighed in substance.' A mere disclosure of more than one alternative does not constitute teaching away unless it criticizes, discredits, or discourages the claimed solution (In re Gurley; In re Fulton). It is improper to combine references where the references teach away from their combination (In re Grasselli). Examiners must consider the totality of the prior art and whether a reference explicitly or implicitly discourages the claimed approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceeding contrary to accepted wisdom is evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed invention proceeds contrary to the accepted wisdom in the art, that fact is evidence tending to show nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Hedges—claimed process used temperatures contrary to those suggested in the art; United States v. Adams—known disadvantages in old devices that would discourage search for new inventions may be taken into account. Known disadvantages or widely held expectations that would discourage arriving at the claimed invention support nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR applies across technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The KSR decision's principles for analyzing obviousness apply across technological fields and are not limited to 'predictable arts'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit has rejected limiting KSR to predictable technologies; examiners should not withdraw an obviousness rejection solely because the invention lies in a field ordinarily considered unpredictable (In re Kubin). The analysis still must account for field‑specific predictability, but KSR's rationales remain applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) common‑ownership/joint research disqualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (as amended 1999/2004/CREATE Act), subject matter developed by another person that qualifies as prior art under certain pre‑AIA 102 subsections shall not preclude patentability if the subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment at the time the claimed invention was made, with a joint research agreement exception when three conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CREATE Act conditions: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. Applicability depends on filing/grant dates (see text): changes apply to patents granted on/after Dec 10, 2004 that are subject to pre‑AIA 102. For reexamination or other procedural situations, examiners must check which version applies (see MPEP § 706.02(l)(1) and related guidance). Note: pre‑AIA 103(c) only disqualifies certain categories of prior art—examiners must ensure statutory prerequisites are met before invoking the disqualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether an application is governed by pre‑AIA or AIA 102/103
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether pre‑AIA or AIA versions of 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 apply depends on the application's filing history and effective filing dates (March 16, 2013 is the AIA effective date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications filed before March 16, 2013 remain governed by pre‑AIA 102/103 even if an RCE or national stage entry is filed after that date; adding new matter on/after March 16, 2013 does not change status. Applications filed on/after March 16, 2013 are AIA applications unless they never contained a claim with an effective filing date on/after that date as defined in 35 U.S.C. 100(i). Examiners should consult MPEP §§ 2131–2138 and § 2159 et seq. to determine which statutory scheme applies to a given application or claim; partial or mixed filing histories may require per‑claim analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) prior art categories
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) provides that a person is not entitled to a patent if the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The categories of prior art for 102(a)(1) include issued patents, published applications, non‑patent printed publications, and evidence of public use or sale. A printed publication that lacks an early enough date to qualify itself may still serve as evidence of an earlier public use or sale. Examiners must use the appropriate documentary or factual evidence to support a 102(a)(1) rejection and identify dates and facts that establish public availability before the effective filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) and 102(d): U.S. patent documents and 'effectively filed' date
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) treats as prior art U.S. patent documents (patents and published applications/deemed publications) that name another inventor and were effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; 35 U.S.C. 102(d) defines when such a U.S. patent document is considered 'effectively filed'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO publications of PCT applications that designate the United States are treated as U.S. patent application publications for 102(a)(2) prior art purposes. Under 102(d), a U.S. patent document is 'effectively filed' as of the earlier of (1) the actual filing date of the patent/application or (2) the filing date of the earliest application (U.S. provisional/nonprovisional, PCT, or foreign) to which benefit/priority is properly claimed and which describes the subject matter relied upon. Examiners must identify the earliest application that adequately describes the relied‑upon subject matter to set the prior‑art effective date.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) one‑year grace period exceptions to (a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure made one year or less before the effective filing date shall not be prior art under 102(a)(1) if (A) the disclosure was made by the inventor or a joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor, or (B) the subject matter had been previously publicly disclosed by the inventor or someone who obtained it from the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one‑year grace period is measured from the filing date of the earliest U.S. or foreign patent application to which a proper benefit or priority claim is asserted and that supports the claimed invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a). This differs from pre‑AIA 102(b), where the measurement was from the filing date of the earliest U.S. application. Examiners must evaluate whether the disclosure falls within the inventor‑originated exceptions and compute the grace period from the correct filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2) exceptions to (a)(2), including ownership exception (102(b)(2)(C))
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure is not prior art under 102(a)(2) if (A) the subject matter was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor, (B) the subject matter had been publicly disclosed by the inventor or one who obtained it from the inventor before the 102(a)(2) effective filing date, or (C) the disclosed subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 102(b)(2)(C) replaces the pre‑AIA 103(c) common‑ownership exception but applies only to prior art under 102(a)(2) (U.S. patent documents), not to 102(a)(1) disclosures (patents, publications, public uses, sales). Examiners must determine whether the ownership/assignment condition is satisfied as of the relevant effective dates and recognize that some disclosures by co‑workers/collaborators may still be prior art under 102(a)(1) unless within a 102(b)(1) exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103: timing and scope of obviousness inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 states that a patent may not be obtained if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AIA shifts the temporal focus of the obviousness inquiry to before the effective filing date (rather than time of invention under pre‑AIA law). The provision tracks pre‑AIA 103(a) in substance and clarifies patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made. Pre‑AIA 103(c) provisions have been replaced by AIA 102(b)(2)(C) and (c); other pre‑AIA exceptions (e.g., 103(b) biotech‑related) were eliminated. Examiners should apply Graham factors and KSR rationales with the effective filing date as the temporal anchor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's duty to state reasons and provide supporting information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office bears the initial burden of explaining why statutory or regulatory requirements have not been met when a claim is rejected; whenever a claim is rejected or an objection made, the Office shall notify the applicant, state the reasons, and provide information and references useful to the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This duty remains unchanged under the AIA. See 35 U.S.C. 132, 37 C.F.R. 1.104(c) and MPEP § 706. Examiners must articulate the factual and legal basis for rejections (e.g., why references are combinable, why a reference qualifies as prior art, computation of effective dates, how teachings of references apply) and supply references or information that assist applicants in assessing the propriety of continuing prosecution.
